title: Weekend plans
title_target: Planes para el fin de semana
goal: Talk about plans with *ir a*, and say months, dates and seasons.
bekal: saying what you're going to do

dialogs.title: Diálogo — ¿Qué vas a hacer?
dialogs.intro: Friday afternoon, the same question all over the world.

lines.speaker: Marta:
lines.text: ¿Qué vas a hacer este fin de semana?
lines.id: What are you doing this weekend?
lines.literal: what you-go to do this end of week?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Voy a visitar a mis abuelos en Bogor.
lines.id: I'm going to visit my grandparents in Bogor.
lines.literal: I-go to visit to my-grandparents in Bogor.

lines.speaker: Marta:
lines.id: How nice! Are you going by train?
lines.literal: how good! you-go to go in train?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Sí, el tren sale a las siete. Quiero llegar temprano.
lines.id: Yes, the train leaves at seven. I want to get there early.
lines.literal: yes, the train it-leaves at the seven. I-want arrive early.

lines.speaker: Marta:
lines.id: How long are you going to stay?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Dos días. Vuelvo el domingo por la tarde.
lines.id: Two days. I'm coming back Sunday afternoon.

lines.speaker: Marta:
lines.text: Aquí va a llover todo el fin de semana.

lines.id: And you? Can't you go out?

lines.text: No, así que voy a ver una serie española en casa.

lines.text: Una de detectives. Te la recomiendo.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Good idea! See you on Monday.

notes: **The future people actually use.** Spanish has an official future tense (*hablaré*), but in everyday conversation people far more often use **ir + a + infinitive**: *voy a estudiar*, *vamos a comer*. For all of A1, this is all you need — just like English "going to".
**Ir looks like nothing else.** *Voy, vas, va, vamos, vais, van* — no connection to the infinitive. Just accept it and learn it; it's one of a handful of truly wild verbs.

**The present can mean later.** *El tren sale a las siete* uses the present even if the train leaves tomorrow. Just like English: "the train leaves at seven". For fixed timetables, the present is actually more usual than *va a salir*.

**People as objects get an "a".** *Visito Bogor* (a place, no *a*), but *visito **a** mis abuelos* (people, with *a*). This little word has no English translation and beginners often forget it — yet native speakers notice right away when it's missing.
**Quedarse** = to stay, to remain. Compare *quedar* (to meet up, arrange) in Unit 16 and *quedar* (to fit, of size) from Unit 13. One word, three lives.
**Cuánto tiempo** = how long. *Tiempo* means both time **and** weather: *no tengo tiempo* (I don't have time), *hace buen tiempo* (the weather's nice).
**¿Cuál?** = "which (one)?", used when choosing from a known set. Compare *¿qué?*, which asks "what" in general: *¿Qué serie ves?* but *¿Cuál prefieres?*
**Nos vemos** literally "we see each other", used exactly like "see you". Compare the more neutral *hasta luego*.

grammars.title: Ir a + infinitive
body: The formula is fixed: a form of *ir* + *a* + the verb in its infinitive (ending in -ar/-er/-ir). The second verb **never** changes:
after: Two other verbs pair up with it because they're also followed directly by an infinitive: *querer* (to want) → *quiero llegar*, and *poder* (can) → *no puedo salir*. These three frame almost every sentence about plans.

*Vamos a…* has a second meaning: an invitation. *Vamos a comer* can mean "we're going to eat" or "let's eat", and only the tone tells them apart. To make the invitation clear, people add *¡Vamos!* in front.

blocks.title: Saying the date
items: The formula is **el + number + de + month**: *el quince de mayo*, *el tres de enero*. Without *de* the sentence doesn't work.

The number is a plain number, not an ordinal: *el dos de mayo* (May 2nd), not *el segundo*. The only one that sometimes differs is the 1st, which can be *el uno* or *el primero* — the second is more common in Latin America.
Months are written in lowercase, just like days: *quince de mayo*, not *quince de Mayo*.
Asking: *¿Qué día es hoy?* (what day) or *¿A qué fecha estamos?* (what date). A full answer: *Hoy es martes, doce de agosto.*

blocks.text: Many tropical countries have only two: *la estación seca* (the dry season) and *la estación de lluvias* (the rainy season). A handy sentence for describing such a country: *En Indonesia no hay cuatro estaciones, solo dos.*

exercises.prompt: Turn these into plans with *ir a*.
Complete with the right form of *querer* or *poder*.

items: It's going to rain this weekend.
We're going to go to the beach by train.
I want to rest at home.
What a shame, I can't make it that day.

answers: Voy a estudiar español. — Vamos a comer en casa. — Marta va a viajar a Madrid. — ¿Vas a trabajar el sábado? — Mis padres van a visitar Bogor. — Vosotros vais a ver una película.
quiero — puedo — queréis — pueden — puedes — queremos
Este fin de semana va a llover. — Vamos a ir a la playa en tren. — Quiero descansar en casa. — Hoy hace mucho calor. — ¿Quedamos a las ocho? — Qué pena, ese día no puedo.
